content.text: A trader I met twice, years apart, told the same story both times with a different ending, and I preferred the second. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself.

At the last oasis the water tasted faintly of salt regardless, a joke the desert never tired of telling. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

The caravan master read the sky the way other men read a ledger, and trusted it about as much. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

A well half remembered is worse than a well forgotten outright, because it invites you to gamble on it. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company.

We crossed the flats at night to spare the animals, and the stars there were more numerous than I had words for. The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both.

The merchant's ledger recorded debts in three languages and grudges, I suspect, in a fourth known only to him. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential.

Salt traders measure distance in wells, not miles, which tells you plainly what the desert considers important. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac.

A rumour from the last oasis reached us garbled, as rumours do, but garbled in a direction that turned out to be true. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own.

The caravan camped a half day short of the crossing rather than risk the flats in failing light. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable.

I have crossed the salt road twice now, and both times arrived a slightly different person than the one who set out. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be.

A guide's reputation rests entirely on wells that are there when he says they will be, and nothing else. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome.

The flats at midday are silent in a way that presses on the ears, absence made almost audible. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order.

We traded cloth for water at the last oasis, a rate the merchant called fair and I called fortunate. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household.

The salt road does not forgive confidence, only preparation, and even then only some of the time. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family.

The salt flats took the light and threw it back doubled, until the horizon stopped meaning anything in particular. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory.

A caravan at dusk moves slower than it does at noon, as though the animals too feel the day loosening its grip. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does.

The well at the crossing was half remembered by every guide who claimed to know it, which worried me more than an honest no. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late.

Merchants kept their ledgers in a shorthand no customs officer ever fully cracked, and none of them explained why. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed.

Rumour travelled faster across the flats than any caravan, arriving at the last oasis a full day ahead of us. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be.

The salt crust cracked under the camels' feet in a sound like distant, patient applause. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made.

The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun.

A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was.

The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried.

An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else. A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing.

The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one. The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two.

A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least. An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar.
